speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Motion agreed to, Bill read the second time, and House went into committee there-otn.
On section 1,

This section deals with witnesses who may oe called to testify on a summary trial before a police magistrate or a justice of the peace. The law as it now stands to my mind and in my experience works injustice, in this way. It provides that a witness may be summoned either on behalf of the Crown or on behalf of the defence; and, unless he appears at the trial in answer to the summons, he may, on proof of service of the summons, be arrested on a warrant and kept in jail until he is called on to testify and he is then liberated. The hardship in cases that have come under my notice is this, that certain witnesses who have been served with summonses in that way have been unable for want of means to travel by public conveyance and have been obliged to walk, sometimes a considerable distance, to attend the court in order to testify. After having testified they do not get their witness fees, sometimes for days or weeks and sometimes they do not get them at all. It rests with the Crown attorney or the prosecuting counsel whether the witness shall get his fees at all or not, and it sometimes turns out, where a witness does not testify in such a manner that his evidence is worth anything, that the crown attorney will refuse to certify for his witness fees. In that way a great hardship is imposed on witnesses. In one instance which came under my notice and which moved me to seek this amendment of the criminal code, a man was served with a summons to attend court who resided seventy-four miles from the court. He had no means and could not come by public conveyance, and he walked, taking two days getting to the court. At the court he testified, upon his testimony a conviction was made and he left the court. Having no means, and having had nothing to eat for a day and a half, he applied to a man on the streets of Belleville to provide for his dinner. He was overheard doing so by an officer, who arrested him for vagrancy and he was taken before the police magistrate before whom he had appeared as a witness and was convicted of vagrancy and con-

fined in the jail, simply because he had not the means to pay his way. on representation to the court, he was subsequently released and a subscription for him was taken up and he was sent home. A case of that kind might happen at any time, and it might just as well be provided that the certificates for his fees should be obtained by the Crown attorney before he attends court, so that he will be provided with the means of attending court. In that way no hardship could be caused to the witness. Under the provisions of this section the witness may attend on a summons if he sees fit to do so, but before he can be arrested for not doing so it must be shown on affidavit or oath to the magistrate that he has been paid his witness fees as fixed by the statute.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
On section 2-section 879 amended.

This section deals with the right of appeal from certain summary convictions. For convenience these may be divided into two classes-those where imprisonment only is imposed and those where a fine is imposed and imprisonment may be inflicted in default of the payment of the fine. The proposed amendment deals with the latter class and it provides for an appeal to the nearest division court of the county in which the cause of complaint arose. Under the provisions of the law at present a conviction by a justice of the peace in Ontario can only be appealed to the court of general sessions of the peace. That court is held twice a year and the costs of an appeal from a conviction in which a fine of say $2 has been inflicted, may amount anywhere from $100 to $150. The object of this amendment is to provide a cheap and quick means of trying such an appeal by providing that it shall be taken to the nearest division court to the place where the cause of complaint arose. In the province of Ontario, according to the way in which division courts are distributed, from 10 to 12 division courts are required to be held in each county so that no person would be obliged to travel more than a few miles to attend such a court, and the witness would not be in attendance more than one day; whereas at present an appellant may be obliged to travel, as in my county, one hundred or one hundred and fifty miles to attend the court of general sessions in the county town. He has to bring his witnesses and keep them there while the county court cases are being tried, perhaps a whole week at very great expense for travel and keep. By this amendment it is proposed to avoid that expense, to do away with the technical features of the appeal that have been established and to make the appeal as cheap, simple and speedy a matter as possible ; so that a person feeling himself aggrieved may file a notice with the clerk of the division court and have his appeal heard at the next sittings of division court in his district. He goes before the same
judge who sits in the court of general sessions, and thus has the advantage of his legal training in either court, and the cost would not be one-twentieth of what it is under the present conditions.
On section 3,
Subsection 2 of the said section S79 is amended by adding after the word ' Renfrew,' in the third line thereof, the words 1 when the conviction adjudges imprisonment only, and in all other cases to the division court of the county of Renfrew held nearest to the place where the cause of the information or complaint arose.'

It has been suggested by a number of county court judges that I should add these words :
Such appeal to be held before a judge of the division court sitting as a judge of the county court.
This is suggested in order that the appeal may be tried in a court of the same magnitude as if the case were brought to the general sessions of the peace.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I would not want to amend the section as I have not considered the amendment.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext:
Section agreed to.
Section 4 and 5 agreed to.
On section 6,
The said section S80 is further amended by inserting the following paragraph immediately after paragraph (c):-
'(cc.) Either party to such appeal may have it tried by jury by giving a notice therefor and by service of such notice upon opposite party or his solicitor and filing the same with the clerk of the court appealed to not less than ten days before the hearing of such appeal, and upon paying such fees and subject to such rules as are prescribed by the court appealed to respecting trials by jury.'

I find that there is a general chorus of disapproval from the county court judges regarding that clause permitting these appeals to be tried by jury. I have given the matter further consideration and I am inclined to think it would be better to expunge that clause.
Section struck out.
Does the promoter of the Bill understand that clause 1, which requires a tender of the witness fees, refers to preliminary investigations as well as trials 1
Yes.

In that case I fear it will create some confusion in the courts in Nova Scotia. In Nova Scotia, we have no person whose duty it is to commence proceedings before the criminal court. The system there is for some person who knows of a crime being committed, to lay the information. This clause would place on

him the burden of furnishing witness fees because there is no fund from which he can draw those fees. After the preliminary investigation is over, the magistrate sends in the account for witness fees to the clerk of the county ; and on the order of the magistrate, the treasurer of the county pays the fees to the witnesses.
Mr. POIiTER. That same practice prevails in Ontario, and the only difference this Bill will make is that instead of the magistrate certifying after the trial, he certifies before the proceedings are begun. If he is satisfied that there is good ground for an investigation, he will have the power to give his certificate to pay the witnesses just the same as he could do it if the Crown Attorney asked him.
Will that not involve an amendment to the Acts of the various provinces because the treasurer of a municipality has no power to pay witness fees in advance ?

As soon as the treasurer of the county receives a certificate from the court he can pay the money, and all this Bill provides is that the certificate can be furnished before the witness testifies instead of after.

It seems to me that this Bill would work an injustice in New Brunswick where the law is much the same as in Nova Scotia. In our courts we have no funds from which to pay witnesses. Any person who considers that an offence has been committed has the right to go before the magistrate and lay the information and the burden is cast upon him of providing his own lawyer and witnesses. Then at the uext session of the county council, the bill is put in, and the county council usually pay these fees. Sometimes they require the certificate of a magistrate or some other official. But there is absolutely no fund on which to draw. Take the case of a person who is too poor to furnish twenty or thirty dollars needed for witness fees. He goes before a magistrate and says : I want to lay information against John Smith. And he wants a dozen witnesses perhaps. The magistrate may issue orders but there is no fund on which to draw for the money, and unless the man is able to furnish the money-and willing too-he would be absolutely out of court, for he cannot compel the attendance of witnesses. He could not have a preliminary examination. A crime of the most hideous character may be committed in New Brunswick and the'person guilty of it, go free because the person laying the information has no way to get the witnesses. Unless some other provision is made this would be a great hindrance to the administration of justice in New Brunswick, and I believe the same is true of Nova Scotia. I do not know what may be the case in Ontario and Mr. SINCLAIR.
; Quebec. I can understand that if this information were laid in a city where the magistrate is in close proximity to the authorities who have the funds, it might be worked out, because there would be time for the magistrate to go to the proper authorities and say :	I believe this is a
case which requires investigation and I ought to have money at my disposal. But, suppose yon have information laid before a magistrate forty miles from the shire town it will be impossible to have the work done in this way. It seems to me that if this Bill is passed an exception ought to be made so far as New Brunswick is concerned because, under our system it would work great injustice.
Do I understand the hon. gentleman (Mr. Carvell) to say that in no case is a witness in a preliminary investigation paid his fees or travelling expenses in his province ?
He is paid from three to six months after ; he is not paid till the meeting of the municipal council. A bill is sent in, and, if it is ordered paid, the secretary-treasurer pays it.
That is on the certificate of the magistrate ?
No ; it depends on whether the municipal council feel that it ought to be paid.
But it is ordered paid on the certificate of the magistrate being presented.

No ; that is only an incident. A man makes out a bill and sends it before the council. I should say it is more generally supported by the certificate of the deputy sheriff or the sheriff. The certificate of the 'magistrate does not necessarily mean that the bill will be paid.

I would point out to the hon. member (Mr. Carvell) that this Bill would not alter that condition of affairs in his province. This does not provide for the payment of witnesses' fees ; that is not the object, but the object is to prevent the arrest of the witness. The witness may go and testify just the same, he may go upon the ordinary summons, just as has been the custom. But this provides that before you can arrest and imprison a witness he must be paid his fees.

It seems to me, notwithstanding the hon. gentleman's (Mr. Porter's) explanation, it amounts to the same thing in the end. We all know how reluctant many people are to attend or to give evidence. This Bill would only be a cloak under which these people could hide in refusing to attend. People learn of these things very quickly. A man would say : I am not in contempt if I do not obey the summons, and a warrant cannot issue for my arrest ; therefore. I will not obey the sum-

mons. The practical result would be that in every case you must tender the conductmoney before the summons would be any good. And there is no way to get the money to tender to the witness so far as New Brunswick is concerned. The result would be that you could not get the witnesses before the magistrate unless the informant, whoever he might be, would put up the money and take the chance of getting it back.

It would not be a very great hardship upon the informant even in the case the hon. gentleman puts, as the present condition may be on the witness, and there is only one informant while there may be many witnesses.

I have had a good deal to do with criminal prosecutions for a good many years in New Brunswick, and I have never found a case where this amendment would be necessary. I am happy to say that the condition referred to by the hon. gentleman does not exist in many places in Canada. It does not exist in New Brunswick ; and I do not think it does in Nova Scotia. I do not think the Bill is so necessary on the ground of urgency as to call upon us to pass it now.

The Bill would be all right if we had a system like that of the United States, where there is an officer called the prosecuting attorney, who has an area of country that he looks after, and whose duty it is to lay information whenever he hears that a crime has been committed, and to provide the means of carrying the prosecution through the court. But we have rather a volunteer system. It is thrown upon the ordinary citizen to prosecute these crimes, and witnesses should take some share in carrying on the criminal business of the country as well as the complainant. It may be as easy for the witness to go and give his evidence as for the prosecutor, who mas'- be a poor man, to pay the witnesses and the prosecuting attorney. It is quite a burden upon the prosecutor to look after the prosecuting attorney. The system pro vided here is a first-rate one if you have a prosecuting attorney in each county. But, under the system we have, this would cause great confusion and would hamper the administration of justice in many parts of the maritime provinces.
I have no desire to impose this legislation upon New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, and am quite satisfied that it should be limited to the province of Ontario.
So far as I am concerned, 1 have no objection. If the people of Ontario want a law like this, that is all right ; but I want the province of New Brunswick exempted from its operations.

speakerposition: Minister of Inland Revenue
speechtext: The criminal law is a general law, and should be made as generally applicable as possible. The provisions should not be confined to one or two provinces. If there is objection to the clause being carried out, as there seems to be in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia and, I am inclined to think, in our province also, it would be better to drop the clause.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: If there is a province where this provision could be made applicable, it would be the province of Quebec, for there the prosecutions i re carried on by the provincial government and not by the municipalities. Of course, it is evident there are objections so far as New Brunswick and Nova Scotia are concerned. But there are exceptional provisions all through the Criminal Code with respect to particular provinces.
In order to test the feeling of the House on the question, I move to reconsider section 1.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I would ask the hon. gentleman if he has consulted the Attorney General for Ontario on this point ?
I have not personally consulted the Attorney General, but I understand from one of the judges that he had a discussion on the matter with him, and he approved generally of the principle of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The other clauses, with the exception of the first, are necessary to give effect to the law we have in force in Ontario, and are applicable exclusively to Ontario. I think the principle is a good one myself, that of saying that tne money should be tendered to a witness in a civil case as well as in a criminal case. Every one who has practised law knows that in a civil case you cannot compel the presence of a witness unless you have tendered him money. In respect to a criminal case I do unt undertand why men who travel a great distance to attend court without having received any consideration whatever in the way of* fees, should be subject to arrest if they do not come. I understand what is said about New Brunswick and Nova Scotia, they appear to have some system that I cannot understand by which a man is not paid for five or six months after he has attended court. If that is the law in New Brunswick it might operate to the injury of the administration of justice.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I would ask the hon. member for West Hastings (Mr. i orter) if he would have any objection to submitting the matter to the Attorney General of Ontario to get his opinion on this point ?-he thinks he has his opinion in a roundabout way through some judge who spoke to the Attorney General.

The matter having been submitted to the Minister of Justice and

having met with his approval, I am willing to abide by his judgment. I do not see any good in delaying the passage of the measure. It is not a matter within the jurisdiction of the Attorney General.

I should think the better way would be to pass the Bill here, as the Minister of Justice approves of it, and then he will submit it to the Attorney General of Ontario if he thinks well to do so. We ought to act on the advice of the Minister of Jus-tic.e

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I do not quite agree with that. I think the member for West Hastings would be consulting his own wishes and perhaps further the object he has in view, if he were to act on my suggestion. The Attorney General for the pro' vince is really the person responsible for the administration of justice, he is the one who speaks for the province. I do not know that it is the duty of the Minister of Justice to communicate with every Attorney General in the Dominion. It may be and it may not be. It is not proposed to have it apply to New Brunswick or Nova Scotia, and exception has been taken to its application in Quebec. For my part I have not the experience that would enable me to express an opinion. Much may be said in support of my hon. friend's contention, but those who have to do with the administration of criminal justice are the ones to advise us. I would again suggest to my hon. friend that he should communicate with the Attorney General of Ontario and get his opinion before proceeding with this clause. I would not wish to vote affirmatively on the measure without knowing the views of the Attorney General.

It appears rather extraordinary that in a matter that is within the jurisdiction of this parliament we should consult the Attorney General as to what his wish may be. We have full jurisdiction here, and if the members of this House believe that the law in its present shape works an injustice to the people of the province of Ontario, I think they should have no hesitation in passing this measure into law. I cannot see why the Postmaster General should insist upon delay. I doubt very much if this parliament consulted the Attorney General when they passed the original clause relating to Ontario, providing that a witness might be arrested if he did not obey the summons served on him in the first instance. I do not know that the Attorney General of Ontario was consulted when we passed that law, and this is merely an amendment of that law, showing that we have full jurisdiction. I would not fear the result in applying to the Attorney General, but I do not see the need of it, and it would delay an act of justice due to the people of Ontario.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Postmaster General
speechtext: I am sorry my hon. friend does not fall in with my suggestion. I should think the hon. member would have come here armed with the opinion of the Attorney General. He says the members of this committee are satisfied to pass this Bill. Perhaps they are, they may be informed as to its merits, but I am an exception. I have no hostility against the measure, I have no opinion on either side at present ; but I think the proper course is to have the advice of the law officer who is responsible for the administration of justice in that province and who has charge of the administration of the criminal law. If the hon. .gentleman himself does not care to communicate with the Attorney General, I am sure the Minister of Justice would be pleased to do so. Until he has done so and the Attorney General's opinion is obtained, 1 must be excused for not supporting the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I think the better course with respect to section 1 would be to allow it to remain in abeyance until we get the opinion of those who are responsible for the administration of criminal justice in each province. I state unhesitatingly, so far as I am personally concerned, after having had twenty years experience in criminal matters, and during a great part of the time as Crown prosecutor for the district and province of Quebec, that it is a hardship that ought to be remedied. For that opinion I cm personally responsible.
If the Minister of Justice thinks it would be wise to get the opinion of the Attorney General I am not going to insist, and am willing to let that clause of the Bill stand.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: May I ask what the question is before the chair ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I may say for the benefit of the leader of the opposition who was not present, that this section relates to the payment of conduct money to a witness attending at a preliminary investigation and trial before a magistrate. The hon. gentleman is aware that in a civil case the tendering of conduct money is a condition precedent to the witness being compelled to attend and give evidence. Under the Criminal Code, even if conduct money is tendered, no matter how poor a man may be or how far he has to go, if he does not attend court he is liable to be imprisoned. This Bill is for the purpose of putting a man who is obliged to attend in a criminal case on the same footing as a man who is obliged to attend in a civil case. The difficulty arises out of the fact that in New Brunswick and Nova Scotia witnesses' fees are paid by the county, as I understand it; it appears that the county is responsible for witnesses' fees, these fees are certified by the magistrate, and they may not be paid for several months after the man has attended court.
If, in a preliminary investigation it was found that the evidence did not justify the charge, and the money is paid out to the witness-what then ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The rule is that the magistrate has control of that. A man lays a complaint before a magistrate. If the magistrate is satisfied that the complaint is of a sufficiently serious character to justify the public assuming the burden of the expenditure that is assumed by the public, but if he decides that it is not of a sufficiently serious character to justify the expenditure being assumed by the public, then the individual has to do it, in which case of course the individual is responsible for file fee.

speakerposition: Minister of Railways and Canals
speechtext:
In New Brunswick, as far as I am familiar with it and I have had quite a number of years' experience, the practice was that at a preliminary investigation witnesses were brought and perhaps the party accused being held for trial in a higher court the witnesses were bound over under bail under a recognizance to appear at the next sitting. They would appear at the higher court and their witness fees would be paid, but the fees incident to the attendance at the preliminary investigation depended entirely on the will and caprice of the county council, and I have seen so many cases of hardship that It appears to me that even if there should be no conduct moneys some steps should be taken whereby men should have some guarantee that their expenses at least would be forthcoming. Now it may be eight or ten months or not five months before the county council meets, and when they do meet if the councillors happen to be in a very happy mood possibly they may pay the bill. It does not depend on the certificate of the magistrate, as the member for Carleton,
N.B. (Mr. Carvell), says. That does not move the council in any way. It is simply a matter of grace on their part. I have a good deal of sympathy with the provision ii' the first clause of this Bill. Perhaps it would be a little drastic to say that the money should be first tendered, but there should be some means of securing the payment on a proper certificate very shortly after the examination. Many cases of hardship have come under my own observation.

This amendment I am ''satisfied will remove the hardship in Ontario. Of course I cannot speak for the other provinces, but I will concur in the suggestion of the Minister of Justice that this Bill be held over until I obtain the opinion of the Attorney General in regard to the matter. I have no objection to that being done with the understanding that I will have the opportunity of bringing up the Bill again. I think the Bill is of such importance that it should be passed at this session if it is to be passed at all.

I notice on referring back to section 580 that the summons refers to the securing of witnesses both on behalf of the prosecution and on the part of the accused. I think this is a branch of the case which requires some consideration. The accused in probably a majority of cases is a poor man and is unable to furnish very many witnesses. It seems to me that if this amendment is passed we will be absolutely placing the accused where he could not get witnesses because if he has not money to tender the conduct money even before the examination, although he might feel that he wished to make a defence at the preliminary investigation, especially if he were innocent-he would say : Why should I go to the higher court and incur twice or three times or four times the expense. I can defend myself before a magistrate. if this Bill became law the defendant would be absolutely debarred from going into his defence unless he happened to have the money necessary to tender the conduct money to the witnesses to bring them before the magistrate. I think that of itself should be sufficient to kill this section of the Bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Is there not a proceeding in forma pauperis?
I will inform the Minister of Justice that out in the country before the country magistrate that proceeding is not very well understood.

In Ontario there is provision by the local law that the judge of a court may certify that a summons issue on the part of the prosecutor or on behalf of a defendant but there is no provision in the statute for the payment of fees. The judge may issue his certificate that a summons be issued by the Crown Attorney or authority summoning that witness to court on behalf of the defence but there is no provision for the payment of the witness. A defendanti if too poor to procure witnesses can get a certificate to subpoena and bring his witnesses to court so there is no hardship in that case at all.
He does not have to advance the fees in this case. But under this amendment he will have to do so.

I want to prevent your putting a witness in jail when he has no means to come to court and has committed no offence.
Amendment (Mr. Carvell) agreed to.
I understand that this Bill will be brought up again.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There are three clauses in this Bill which are necessary and which I will have to introduce myself in order to give effect to the Criminal Code

unless they are proceeded with by my hon. friend.

speakerposition: Minister of Militia and Defence
speechtext: Perhaps it might be worth while, if the Minister of Justice can accomplish it, to have a memorandum prepared as to the law in the different provinces. I think in Nova Scotia it is as the Minister of Justice has mentioned, not only at a preliminary investigation but at the formal trial later on. I do not know by whom the fees are paid in Ontario and Quebec. Are they paid by the local government ?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: They are paid by the local government in Quebec.
They are paid by the county treasurers in Ontario.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: They are not paid out of the fees of the local government.
The local government pays part of the expense.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: The magistrate determines as to the proper charge.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Tuesday, April 11, 1905.
